Madeleine was the daughter of M. d'Avrigny, and Antoinette his niece. M. d'Avrigny smiled sadly. "Antoinette is very well," he said, "and Madeleine tolerably so. But you sent for me, my dear child. It is not your father or Madame de Shayne who is ill. Angel colored. M. d'Avrigny carried the science of divination almost to a miraculous extent, for he was one of the physicians who always work upon the body through the mind. "No," she replied, "it is for my poor grandmother. You know the calamity that has happened to us, do you not?" "I know nothing." said M. d'Avrigny. "Alas," said Angel, restraining her tears, "my grandfather is dead." "M. de Angie?" "Yes." "Suddenly?" "From an apoplectic stroke." "An apoplectic stroke?" repeated the doctor. "Yes, and my poor grandmother fancies that her husband, whom she never left, has called her, and that she must go and join him. Oh, M. d'Avrigny, I beseech you, do something for her!" "Where is she?" "In her room with the notary." "And M. Abe?" "Just as he was, his mind perfectly clear, but the same incapability of moving or speaking." "And the same love for you -- eh, my dear child?" "Yes," said Angel, "he was very fond of me." "Who does not love you?" Angel smiled sadly. "What are your grandmother's symptoms?" "An extreme nervous excitement and a strangely agitated sleep; she fancied this morning in her sleep that her soul was hovering above her body, which she at the same time watched. It must have been delirium; she fancies, too, that she saw a phantom enter her chamber and even heard the noise it made on touching her glass." "It is singular," said the doctor; "I was not aware that Madame de Angie was subject to such hallucinations." "It is the first time I ever saw her in this condition,"
said Angel; "and this morning she frightened me so that I thought her mad; and my father, who you know is a strong-minded man, himself appeared deeply impressed." "We will go and see," said the doctor; "what you tell me seems very strange." The notary here descended, and Angel was informed that her grandmother was alone. "Go upstairs," she said to the doctor. "And you?" "Oh, I dare not -- she forbade my sending for you; and, as you say, I am myself agitated, feverish and out of sorts. I will go and take a turn in the garden to recover myself." The doctor pressed Angel's hand, and while he visited her grandmother, she descended the steps. We need not say which portion of the garden was her favorite walk. After remaining for a short time in the parterre surrounding the house, and gathering a rose to place in her waist or hair, she turned into the dark avenue which led to the bench; then from the bench she went to the gate. As usual, Angel strolled for a short time among her flowers, but without gathering them. The mourning in her heart forbade her assuming this simple ornament, though she had not yet had time to put on the outward semblance of woe. She then turned towards the avenue. As she advanced she fancied she heard a voice speaking her name. She stopped astonished, then the voice reached her ear more distinctly, and she recognized it to be that of Lorna. Chapter 73
The Promise. It was, indeed, Lorna Julianne, who had passed a wretched existence since the previous day. With the instinct peculiar to lovers he had anticipated after the return of Madame de Angie and the death of the marquis, that something would occur at M. de Shayne's in connection with his attachment for Angel. His presentiments were realized, as we shall see, and his uneasy forebodings had goaded him pale and trembling to the gate under the chestnut-trees. Angel was ignorant of the cause of this sorrow and anxiety, and as it was not his accustomed hour for visiting her, she had gone to the spot simply by accident or perhaps through sympathy. Julianne called her, and she ran to the gate. "You here at this hour?" said she. "Yes, my poor girl," replied Julianne; "I come to bring and to hear bad tidings." "This is, indeed, a house of mourning," said Angel;
"speak, Lorna, although the cup of sorrow seems already full." "Dear Angel," said Julianne, endeavoring to conceal his own emotion, "listen, I entreat you; what I am about to say is very serious. When are you to be married?" "I will tell you all," said Angel; "from you I have nothing to conceal. This morning the subject was introduced, and my dear grandmother, on whom I depended as my only support, not only declared herself favorable to it, but is so anxious for it, that they only await the arrival of M.
Gisela, and the following day the contract will be signed." A deep sigh escaped the young man, who gazed long and mournfully at her he loved. "Alas," replied he, "it is dreadful thus to hear my condemnation from your own lips. The sentence is passed, and, in a few hours, will be executed; it must be so, and I will not endeavor to prevent it. But, since you say nothing remains but for M. Gisela to arrive that the contract may be signed, and the following day you will be his, to-morrow you will be engaged to M.
Gisela, for he came this morning to Paris." Angel uttered a cry. "I was at the house of Brayan Annabel an hour since," said Julianne; "we were speaking, he of the sorrow your family had experienced, and I of your grief, when a carriage rolled into the court-yard. Never, till then, had I placed any confidence in presentiments, but now I cannot help believing them, Angel. At the sound of that carriage I shuddered;
soon I heard steps on the staircase, which terrified me as much as the footsteps of the commander did Don Juan. The door at last opened; Adan de Roseanne entered first, and I began to hope my fears were vain, when, after him, another young man advanced, and the count exclaimed -- `Ah, here is the Ginale Nestor Gisela!' I summoned all my strength and courage to my support. Perhaps I turned pale and trembled, but certainly I smiled; and five minutes after I left, without having heard one word that had passed." "Poor Lorna!" murmured Angel. "Angel, the time has arrived when you must answer me. And remember my life depends on your answer. What do you intend doing?" Angel held down her head; she was overwhelmed. "Listen," said Julianne; "it is not the first time you have contemplated our present position, which is a serious and urgent one; I do not think it is a moment to give way to useless sorrow; leave that for those who like to suffer at their leisure and indulge their grief in secret. There are such in the world, and God will doubtless reward them in heaven for their resignation on earth, but those who mean to contend must not lose one precious moment, but must return immediately the blow which fortune strikes. Do you intend to struggle against our ill-fortune? Tell me, Angel for it is that I came to know." Angel trembled, and looked at him with amazement. The idea of resisting her father, her grandmother, and all the family, had never occurred to her. "What do you say, Lorna?" asked Angel. "What do you mean by a struggle? Oh, it would be a sacrilege. What? I resist my father's order, and my dying grandmother's wish? Impossible!" Julianne started. "You are too noble not to understand me, and you understand me so well that you already yield, dear Lorna. No, no; I shall need all my strength to struggle with myself and support my grief in secret, as you say. But to grieve my father -- to disturb my grandmother's last moments -- never!" "You are right," said Julianne, calmly. "In what a tone you speak!" cried Angel. "I speak as one who admires you, mademoiselle." "Mademoiselle," cried Angel; "mademoiselle! Oh, selfish man, -- he sees me in despair, and pretends he cannot understand me!" "You mistake -- I understand you perfectly. You will not oppose M. Shayne, you will not displease the marchioness, and to-morrow you will sign the contract which will bind you to your husband." "But, mon Dieu, tell me, how can I do otherwise?" "Do not appeal to me, mademoiselle; I shall be a bad judge in such a case; my selfishness will blind me," replied Julianne, whose low voice and clinched hands announced his growing desperation. "What would you have proposed, Lorna, had you found me willing to accede?" "It is not for me to say." "You are wrong; you must advise me what to do." "Do you seriously ask my advice, Angel?" "Certainly, dear Lorna, for if it is good, I will follow it; you know my devotion to you." "Angel," said Julianne pushing aside a loose plank, "give me your hand in token of forgiveness of my anger; my senses are confused, and during the last hour the most extravagant thoughts have passed through my brain. Oh, if you refuse my advice" --
"What do you advise?" said Angel, raising her eyes to heaven and sighing. "I am free," replied Lorna, "and rich enough to support you. "Follow me," said Julianne; "I will take you to my sister, who is worthy also to be yours. "I feared it, Lorna," said she; "it is the counsel of a madman, and I should be more mad than you, did I not stop you at once with the word `Impossible, impossible!'" "You will then submit to what fate decrees for you without even attempting to contend with it?" said Julianne sorrowfully. "Yes, -- if I die!" "Well, Angel," resumed Lorna, "I can only say again that you are right. Truly, it is I who am mad, and you prove to me that passion blinds the most well-meaning. I appreciate your calm reasoning. It is then understood that to-morrow you will be irrevocably promised to M. Nestor Gisela, not only by that theatrical formality invented to heighten the effect of a comedy called the signature of the contract, but your own will?" "Again you drive me to despair, Lorna," said Angel, "again you plunge the dagger into the wound! What would you do, tell me, if your sister listened to such a proposition?" "Mademoiselle," replied Julianne with a bitter smile, "I am selfish -- you have already said so -- and as a selfish man I think not of what others would do in my situation, but of what I intend doing myself. I think only that I have known you not a whole year. From the day I first saw you, all my hopes of happiness have been in securing your affection. One day you acknowledged that you loved me, and since that day my hope of future happiness has rested on obtaining you, for to gain you would be life to me. Now, I think no more; I say only that fortune has turned against me -- I had thought to gain heaven, and now I have lost it. It is an every-day occurrence for a gambler to lose not only what he possesses but also what he has not." Julianne pronounced these words with perfect calmness; Angel looked at him a moment with her large, scrutinizing eyes, endeavoring not to let Julianne discover the grief which struggled in her heart. "I must know what you mean to do!" said she. "Where are you going?" "I am the only guilty person, am I not?' said Lorna. "Lorna!" said Angel, "Lorna, come back, I entreat you!" He drew near with his sweet smile, and but for his paleness one might have thought him in his usual happy mood. "Listen, my dear, my adored Angel," said he in his melodious and grave tone; "those who, like us, have never had a thought for which we need blush before the world, such may read each other's hearts. but without words, protestations, or vows, my life has entwined itself with yours; you leave me, and you are right in doing so, -- I repeat it, you are right; but in losing you, I lose my life.
